title: Kuku Sabzi
subtitle: Persian herb frittata
excerpt: Kuku sabzi is a Persian herb-packed frittata eaten at Nowruz, the Persian New Year. The high ratio of herbs to eggs gives it a dense, almost cake-like texture unlike a typical omelette. It is equally good warm from the pan or served at room temperature the following day.
sourceNotes: Kuku sabzi is a Persian herb-packed frittata eaten at Nowruz, the Persian New Year. The high ratio of herbs to eggs gives it a dense, almost cake-like texture unlike a typical omelette.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Kuku sabzi can be made up to 2 days ahead and served at room temperature. It keeps well in the refrigerator.

content.text: Unlike a French omelette or Italian frittata, kuku sabzi is almost more herb than egg: the herbs are the filling, not a garnish. Chop everything finely and pack it in without hesitation. The turmeric and cumin give a warm, earthy backbone to what would otherwise be a very green, grassy flavour. Traditionally kuku sabzi also contains dill and chives, both finely chopped. Add a handful of each if you have them. Walnuts and barberries are classic garnishes: scatter over the top before serving if available.
Crack the eggs into a large bowl and whisk well until the yolks and whites are fully combined. Season generously with salt and black pepper.
Add the turmeric and cumin to the eggs and whisk again to distribute the spices evenly throughout the mixture.
Stir the chopped parsley, coriander, and spring onions into the egg mixture. The bowl should look predominantly green with the eggs barely visible.
Melt the butter in a 26 cm frying pan over a medium-low heat. Swirl to coat the base and sides of the pan.

Pour in the herb and egg mixture and spread it level with a spatula. Reduce the heat to low, cover with a lid or a sheet of foil, and cook for 15 to 18 minutes until the edges are set and the centre is only just wobbly.

To cook the top, place a large plate over the pan and invert the kuku onto the plate in one confident movement. Slide it back into the pan, uncooked-side down, and cook for a further 4 to 5 minutes until set through.
Slide the kuku onto a board or serving plate and leave to cool for at least 5 minutes before cutting into wedges. Serve warm or at room temperature.

items.symptom: The kuku sticks when I try to flip it
items.cause: The pan may not have been coated thoroughly with butter, or the heat was too high and the base set before the butter could work as a release.
items.fix: Run a flexible spatula around the edge and underneath before attempting to flip. Use a plate slightly larger than the pan and flip quickly with confidence.

items.symptom: The centre is still runny after the cooking time
items.cause: The heat was too high, which set the outside quickly while the centre stayed liquid. Kuku needs gentle, sustained heat.
items.fix: Return the pan to a low heat, cover again, and give it another 5 minutes. Check again: the centre should feel firm when lightly pressed.

items.cause: Fresh herbs need a good amount of salt to come to life, and the eggs absorb seasoning less readily once cooked.
items.fix: Season more assertively at the egg-whisking stage next time. Serve with a pinch of flaky salt and a squeeze of lemon on the finished wedges.
